The 'Otaimatsu' Torch Ritual at the Flower Festival: Shuni-e at Shinyakushi-ji Temple
April 8th, the day of the Flower Festival. As dusk approached, I set out again and headed to Shinyakushi-ji Temple in Takahata-cho.

Shinyakushi-ji, known for its National Treasure Twelve Heavenly Generals, was founded by Empress Komyo to pray for the recovery of Emperor Shomu from illness. The Emperor subsequently recovered. The temple's name, which means 'Temple of the New Yakushi,' comes from the fact that it enshrines the miraculous Yakushi Nyorai (Medicine Buddha).

As can be understood from this history, Shinyakushi-ji has a deep connection with Todai-ji Temple; it still belongs to the Kegon sect and is considered a branch temple. And, just like the Shuni-e at Todai-ji's Nigatsu-do Hall, the Shuni-e is held here at Shinyakushi-ji, and the Otaimatsu torches are lit.

People waiting for the Otaimatsu torches in front of the Shinyakushi-ji Main Hall (Nara period, National Treasure). A repentance service is currently being held inside the hall. Cherry blossom petals are gathered along the edge of the stone pavement.

The main rites of the Shuni-e at Nigatsu-do, known as 'Omizutori,' take place from March 1st until the early hours of March 14th. While that is a very long event, the Shuni-e at Shinyakushi-ji is held only on April 8th. The 8th of every month is the memorial day of Yakushi Nyorai.
Compared to that, the scale is reduced and compressed in many ways, but there is one point where it is equal to Nigatsu-do: the size of the Otaimatsu torches.
